stories.title: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
stories.summary: Image source, EPA Image caption, Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi By Wycliffe Muia Published 10 October 2026, 01:00 BST A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October. That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.

stories.summary: Fraught with danger … Jasmine Jobson in In the Shadows View image in fullscreen Fraught with danger … Jasmine Jobson in In the Shadows Review In the Shadows review – true tale of Ramla Ali’s remarkable rise through the boxing ranks is a knockout Jasmine Jobson goes the distance as the British-Somalian boxer battling pain from her past and her family’s disapproval in a heavyweight, tick-the-boxes production T he true-life success story of boxer Ramla Ali is confidently told in this capable picture from screenwriter Ursula Rani Sarma and documentary director Anthony Wonke, in his feature-film debut. Ali is the British-Somali boxer who escaped to the UK from the Somali civil war with her family as a refugee, and in 2021 became the first person to box for Somalia at Olympic Games . The boxing significance of her last name is actually not mentioned in the film – and I never noticed it until it flashed up in a kind of “fight card” intertitle before her first competitive bout. She is fiercely played by Jasmine Jobson, from TV’s Top Boy; her supportive white Muslim-convert husband Richard – a hugely important figure in enabling Ramla to break away from her disapproving family and do as she wants – is played by Finn Cole, and her abusive trainer Clinton is Gershwyn Eustache Jr. This is a film that takes you through the classic boxing-movie scenes fluently enough: the nervous first appearance in the gym, the overbearing quasi-parental coach, the heartstopping fight debut.

stories.summary: South Africa: High Court Orders ANC to Reinstate Andile Lungisa After Unlawful Removal 9 October 2026 Daily Maverick (Johannesburg) By Nonkululeko Njilo With elections less than a month away, the high court has ruled that the ANC's removal of Andile Lungisa from its Nelson Mandela Bay candidate list is unlawful, ordering the party to reinstate his name and pay his legal costs. The ANC has been left with egg on its face after the high court ruled that its decision to remove mayoral hopeful Andile Lungisa from its candidate list for Nelson Mandela Bay was unlawful and unconstitutional, finding that the party had failed to justify his removal shortly before the candidate-nomination deadline. In a judgment handed down on Friday, 9 October, Judge Nelisa Mali ordered the ANC to reinstate Lungisa on its internal proportional representation candidate list and directed the party to submit his name to the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) if the law permits it to supplement its list. Lungisa had accused party Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula of removing his name after the ANC's candidate-selection process had advanced to its final stages. However, the court did not find Mbalula personally liable.

stories.summary: Africa: Vaccines Deliver Over U.S.$30 Billion in Economic Benefits for Lower-Income Countries in 2025 9 October 2026 GAVI Alliance (Geneva) Gavi-supported immunisation generated more than US$ 30 billion in economic benefits in 2025, through lower healthcare costs and healthier, more productive populations Recognising the value of immunisation, countries invested a record US$ 301 million in co-financing of Gavi-supported vaccines in 2025 Dr Sania Nishtar, Gavi CEO: "When it comes to immunisation we know that the return on investment extends far beyond health to supporting sustainable, inclusive economic growth." Geneva, 7 October 2026 – Vaccine programmes supported by Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance (Gavi) generated more than US$ 30 billion in economic benefits in 2025, the highest annual total in the Alliance's history, according to Gavi's annual report published today . These gains came from preventing illness, death and long-term disability, sparing countries healthcare and wider societal costs, and ultimately helping children achieve higher educational attainment, leading to a longer, more productive working life. In the same year, lower-income countries contributed a record US$ 301 million towards the cost of Gavi-supported vaccines through Gavi's co-financing model, under which countries progressively assume a greater share of vaccine costs as their economies grow. This reflects a broader trajectory: over the last five years, countries have matched the total they contributed over the previous 13 years combined, and from 2026–2030 implementing countries are projected to fund nearly 50% of the costs of their vaccines. Unrest broke out on Thursday in Soweto, a sprawling township outside Johannesburg, the country's largest city, and Durban, a major port on the east coast. The violence comes amid growing anger over a court ruling which would allow some migrants who had arrived in the country illegally to apply for asylum. This had led to long queues outside immigration centres and the government on Friday said it would change the way it would comply with that ruling, without giving details. The Department of Home Affairs said the current policy had seen its staff "overwhelmed", while "serious threats to public safety and order had emerged".

Photograph: Reuters The Guardian view on Ethiopia’s return to conflict: civilian catastrophe and a spiralling regional polycrisis Editorial The escalating violence reflects deep domestic rifts – but is fuelled by broader geopolitical power games W hen the Nobel peace laureate is announced on Friday, the committee will be hoping that its choice ages better than 2019’s. Ethiopia’s prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, won the prize for ending the 20-year border conflict with neighbouring Eritrea – signing a peace agreement with President Isaias Afwerki. A year later, their new relationship facilitated a war with the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) that killed as many as 600,000 people, displaced millions more, led to atrocities by both sides, and pushed Tigrayans into famine .

Military vehicles carrying soldiers drove across Eritrea’s southern border into Tigray on Wednesday, reaching the town of Adigrat 25 miles (40km) south, according to civilian witnesses, a militia commander and the conflict monitoring group Acled. Eritrean troops were then targeted by Ethiopian government drones on Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, Acled said.

Cette avocate sud-africaine, ancienne militante contre la politique d'apartheid, s'est illustrée dans la lutte pour les droits humains et contre l'impunité des perpétrateurs de crimes contre l'humanité et de génocide. L'intéressée n'a pas tardé à réagir, non sans humour : "Si vous applaudissez un peu plus fort, je partagerai peut-être le prix avec Trump", en référence à la campagne incessante menée par le président américain pour obtenir le prix. • Alors que des troupes érythréennes ont passé mercredi la frontière au nord de l'Éthiopie pour venir en soutien aux rebelles du Tigré, les forces éthiopiennes ont répliqué à grand renfort de drones. Cette reprise de Kidal, bastion de la rébellion, représente une victoire pour l'armée malienne, qui en avait été chassée en avril par le Front de libération de l'Azawad (FLA) et ses alliés jihadistes du Groupe de soutien à l'islam et aux musulmans (JNIM), affilié à Al-Qaïda . • Qui du Maroc ou du Sénégal sera champion d'Afrique ?

stories.title: Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa
stories.summary: Image source, Zanu-PF Image caption, Wicknell Chivayo, who had a fleet of personalised luxury cars, loved white Rolls-Royces By Ish Mafundikwa Reporting from Harare Published 8 October 2026 Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death. He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes. He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving. Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes. His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune.

stories.title: Africa: Africa's Non-Communicable Diseases Burden Continues to Rise, Latest Study Finds
stories.summary: Africa's Non-Communicable Diseases Burden Continues to Rise, Latest Study Finds 5 October 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Addis Ababa) A 2026 Lancet Global Health analysis using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 data finds that non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are accounting for a growing share of Africa's health burden. In 2023, NCDs resulted in an estimated 263 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), with one DALY representing one year of healthy life lost. NCDs caused an estimated 2.33 billion cases and 4.70 million deaths. The leading causes of NCD deaths in 2023 were, Ischaemic heart disease - 801,000 deaths, stroke - 700,000, chronic kidney disease - 293,000, hypertensive heart disease - 246,000 and diabetes - 245,000. The three largest contributors to NCD deaths were high systolic blood pressure - 26.2% dietary risks - 14.7%, air pollution - 14.2%.

stories.title: ‘There’s always been a belittling of African women’: honouring history’s invisible heroines
stories.summary: As demand for it drove the transatlantic slave trade, sugar symbolises the sacrifice of people for goods. Photograph: Pamela Tulizo Congolese photographer Pamela Tulizo uses costume and vivid scenery to celebrate women’s strength and give a new perspective on slavery By Sarah Johnson P amela Tulizo’s latest series of photographs started with a question. “I asked myself, why are women in my community in particular, and African women in general, so strong?” says Tulizo, an artist and photographer from the Democratic Republic of the Congo . “Where does this strength come from?” Growing up in Goma in eastern DRC, Tulizo was informed and inspired by the women she was surrounded by, including her mother, her sisters, her mother’s friends and her neighbours. Years later, when she began to look into the role of women throughout African history, she says: “I realised that perhaps women have been forced to be strong since the dawn of time, forced by circumstance to build that resilience.” View image in fullscreen Women are placed at the centre of the series of 23 staged photographs Her research brought her to slavery, the “cruellest period in human history”, which is often just associated with the men who were forced across oceans to form workforces abroad. Women, she noticed, were largely invisible, their stories untold. With that in mind, Tulizo placed women at the centre of her series of 23 staged photographs called Mababu (“ancestors” in Swahili).

stories.title: Anthropic report: Is Russia using AI for disinformation in the Central African Republic and elsewhere across Africa?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NTaF The Claude app was allegedly misused by Russian agents Image: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement In Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic , Russian agents are said to have deliberately used the AI assistant Claude to promote pro-Russian influence. A report titled " Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI ," published by US-based company Anthropic in September, detailed how opposition politicians were monitored, propaganda content was created and disinformation campaigns were supported. The report claimed that Claude was used primarily to produce content broadcast by Radio Lengo Songo, a radio station that, according to the international investigative collective All Eyes on Wagner, is funded by Russia. The collective, made up of journalists, academics and experts, investigates the activities of the Russian mercenary Wagner Group and its successor structures, such as the Africa Corps, around the world. Pro-Russian propaganda, surveillance of the opposition The Anthropic report said the content was pro-Russian and portrayed the Central African government and the Africa Corps mercenaries in a positive light, while taking a critical stance on France and the opposition.

stories.title: Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
stories.summary: Figure caption, Boateng Bismark James has been preaching on buses leaving Neoplan station since 2023 By Thomas Naadi BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Accra Published 4 October 2026 Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country. Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana. Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread. On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel. Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices.
